I'm assuming everyone's read the written submission, so I'll try not to repeat too
much of it. For people who haven't met me before, I'm Eleanor Parks
from ECPAT New Zealand. We've obviously been watching very closely
since late 2025, when Section 17 was
suspended under urgency. Overseas adoptions are
very much in our wheelhouse. We're an anti-trafficking organization,
and so cases like Matamata and more recently the Tuai
case have demonstrated how these informal pathways really can be
weaponized for modern slavery. So we're very supportive of the fact that
the government is looking into address these loopholes and
do something about them.
For a bit of background, part of ECPAT International, so the largest
network of organizations working to end child sexual
exploitation and trafficking. That is the specific focus.
And our work in New Zealand is very much grounded in research,
advocacy, and lived experience of young people here and
frontline workers like social workers here.
We've consistently focused on safeguarding children from
exploitation and domestic trafficking and international trafficking.
So that includes things like the misuse of adoption practices.
What we do know is that while cases of child trafficking in New
Zealand rarely make headlines, there are also the many, many stories of
successful, life-changing cross-border support for children,
stories where children have been provided with safety and family and
opportunity, that don't make headlines.
And so our challenge and your challenge is to stop the abuse,
the cases of abuse and exploitation, but without stopping those
good, positive cases that are giving these children what they really
need to be safe and to thrive. And at the moment, this
bill, while very well intended, isn't quite hitting that mark.
So I'd like to go into a few details around some of our concerns.
So we definitely are supporting strong protections.
We want to prevent child trafficking, and we want to stop overseas
adoption processes from being misused.
And we want effective scrutiny where there are child
protection concerns.
But at the moment, the framework in its current form would likely
unintentionally deny certain children access to care,
family support, education, health services, and
stable living arrangements
if they do not come from a country that has yet been designated
under a future regulatory process.
So
looking at Section 17 just as a trafficking loophole
misreads a pathway that has also enabled
legitimate Pacific kinship care based in cross-border
family support, and these are the children that we're concerned will be missing
out on that safety and security.
A few details on that. On the
surface, the provisions definitely look to reduce the risk of
adoption being used inappropriately for
immigration or exploitation,
but it doesn't make a distinction between adoptions that are
undertaken to secure those immigration outcomes and facilitate
abuse and adoption that is being used as the
genuine kinship care arrangements that are in the best
interests of the child.
In a Western view, adoption is seen as a solution
for a child with no family or no suitable family,
and Western adoption laws, including the Hague Convention, which has been a big
part of this conversation, are built on that clean break
idea. The child is removed from unsuitable parents and transplanted to
better ones. But in the Pacific, adoption is
often additive.
We're not replacing children's parents with better ones.
It's about gaining additional caregivers.
At the moment, the proposed amendments really impose that
Western nuclear family model
in places that don't necessarily fit, that don't align with
Pacific ways of understanding family.
In the Pacific, these kinds of care, this kinship customary care, is
recognized and it's a valued practice, with children moving between households and
communities and countries within their family
networks. And it's not about
circumventing immigration rules.
It's about welfare, it's about education, it's about support.
And this applies to a lot of children in New Zealand.
It's estimated that 3.2% or as much as
5% of all children in New Zealand are
living in kinship care arrangements outside of
formal statutory care.
Kinship care isn't a risk factor, it's a protective
asset.
We want to be careful not to be removing the protective
aspect.
What we need is to reconcile
The best interests of the child as the primary
consideration,
and it's just not quite happening yet.
So any legislative framework governing overseas adoptions,
they do need to be measured against our obligations
under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
So that includes the best interests of the child, preservation of family
relationships, which covers the importance of family
relationships, identity, and appropriate alternative care.
It says that legislation should avoid unnecessarily disrupting family-based
care arrangements where safeguards can be demonstrated.
And it also covers protection from exploitation, of course.
But those safeguards need to be targeted at identifying the risk where it actually
exists, which is very often at the level of the individual
caring arrangement in the receiving country.
So
not only focusing on where the children are coming from, but focusing
on what are the child protection
arrangements here in New Zealand when those children are here.
We can't just be monitoring what is happening in the sending
countries if the abuse is happening here, which is what we've seen.

back to a summary from you?

provision dealing specifically with kinship care

kinship care arrangements, such as those common in Pacific

be slowed down

this in place for the longer term without those other
additional factors.

addressing the committee regarding the bill's limitations on the
Family Court's jurisdiction. And the society's concerns around this
limitation are twofold. The bill introduces
barriers that firstly prevent the Family Court from recognizing
genuine parent-child relationships, even where that's in the child's
interest to do so. And secondly, it creates a
barrier to the court carrying out its very important protective
function.
In cases where there is not an international surrogacy or where the
parties and child are not all ordinarily resident to New Zealand,
the bill really narrows access to the court's expertise by imposing
this very high three-pronged cumulative threshold.
And it goes even further because the bill also creates situations where there's no
pathway to the court at all, where both the child and the adoptive
parents are living overseas.
And we consider that these jurisdictional restrictions in the bill are really
inconsistent with the fundamentally child-centered
approach that should underpin all adoption decisions, indeed all
decisions affecting children, in line with the United Nations
Convention on the Rights of the Child.
We think it's really important to remember that our Family Court has spent more
than 70 years determining adoption applications through
a child-centered process that's really focused on the welfare and the
best interests of the child. Throughout that time, the court
has evolved, and it's been really nimble in interpreting the
legislation to meet the changing social needs of the
families that come before it.
The court is undertaking the very inquiries and
tests that Parliament is concerned are not happening in non-designated
countries, and it's uniquely equipped to identify
unsafe arrangements, assess consent, scrutinize the
evidence, and where necessary, refuse inappropriate
applications.
As I mentioned earlier, some children will be excluded from the court's
consideration altogether, not because the adoption is
unsafe, but because that statutory gateway is just simply too
restrictive. And the consequence will be that some children of New
Zealanders may be unable to secure legal recognition
of the parent-child relationship, even when that's plainly in that child's
best interest. And that's likely to create adverse
situations where some children face very different outcomes from their
siblings solely because they were adopted rather than being born
into the family. And at paragraph 4.15 of our
submission, we outline two real-life
examples of where that would happen.
So it's this society's submission that there needs to remain a pathway
for the courts to consider such cases, again, particularly where
doing so will promote the welfare of the child.
Ultimately, it's our view that the child bears the consequences of this bill.
Children don't choose the circumstances of their birth, they don't choose where
they are born and where they live, and they certainly do not choose the legal
arrangements made by adults. But under this bill,
some of those children will be left without appropriate legal recognition of their
parentage and the consequences that come with that.
The consequences being denial to that child of legal recognition
of their parentage, denial of security of status,
denial of inheritance rights, and denial of a really clear
pathway to citizenship and united family life.
Our submission isn't that safeguards should be weakened.
It is that when you limit the jurisdictional access to the court, a really
important safeguard is being diminished.
The court remains a strong guard against trafficking, coercion, and
exploitation. And further, by limiting the court's jurisdiction, you're
creating this pendulum swing that creates other risks for children
because, as we've said, some children will lose the meaningful ability
to come before the court and have the court consider their individual
case on their merits in order to avoid unintended
consequences.
Paragraph 4.24 of our submission summarizes our
recommendations for mitigating these risks and
these concerns, and those proposed
amendments are really aimed at achieving the
necessary balance. As Margaret said earlier, we don't need to choose
between different risks here or different categories of
children. We can achieve a balance.

hands. Yeah.
